citations.evidenceText:
Traditional versus Evolutionary Search
•   Traditional optimization methods face significant drawbacks:
   – Local Minima: Traditional methods are highly sensitive to the initial starting
       point, and a search starting in a local basin can get stuck in local optima,
       missing the global optimum.
   – Discontinuity: Gradient-based traditional methods fail when the objective
       function is discontinuous, as gradients cannot be computed at discontinuities.
   – Search Robustness: Most traditional methods are not suitable for parallel
      computing or a wide variety of problem types.
•  The Evolutionary Advantage:
   – Genetic Algorithms (GAs) provide a robust alternative
       as they start with a population of random solutions.
   –  If any one solution enters the global minima basin
      through crossover or mutation, it reaches the global
     optimum and avoid getting trapped in local minima.

citations.evidenceText:
What Is a Genetic Algorithm (GA)?
•  GA is a search and optimization method inspired by natural evolution. It starts
   from a population of candidate solutions and improves them generation after
   generation using the ideas of selection, reproduction, and mutation.
•   It provides computationally tractable, robust, and adaptive solutions to complex
   real-world problems where traditional "hard computing" methods may fail due
   to high non-linearity or ill-defined mathematical models.
•  Basic principles:
   – Iterative Search: Explores the search space through successive generations
       to find the best feasible solution.
   – Probabilistic Nature: Unlike deterministic algorithms,
     GAs use randomness to guide a directed search of the
       solution space.
   – Population-Based: Search starts with a population of
         initial solutions generated at random, rather than a single point.

•  Binary-coded GAs suffer from the Hamming Cliff, where adjacent numerical

concepts.title: Scope of Gray-code benefit
concepts.description: The one-bit adjacency of consecutive Gray values is not a converse guarantee for every possible bit flip. The provided lookup supplies a concrete counterexample.

concepts.title: GA working cycle
concepts.description: Evaluation informs parent selection; crossover and mutation create the next candidates.

concepts.title: Literal stopping-flow limitation
concepts.description: The schematic omits a final evaluation on the exit branch. A practical implementation must evaluate the returned population or preserve an evaluated best-so-far record; do not silently invent a box in the source.

concepts.title: Population size and repeated selection
concepts.description: Selection with replacement can produce repeated high-fitness candidates while retaining a fixed pool size.

concepts.title: Roulette probabilities and expected copies
concepts.description: Roulette selection is proportional to fitness; an expectation does not force a particular sample.

concepts.title: Validity of raw roulette weights
concepts.description: Use valid nonnegative selection weights with positive total; raw minimized costs or negative scores require an explicit transformation or another selection scheme.

concepts.title: Rank-based probabilities
concepts.description: Rank selection depends on ordering rather than the raw score gap.

concepts.title: Fitness scaling and ranks
concepts.description: Rank selection is invariant to strictly order-preserving score changes, while raw proportional probabilities need not be.

concepts.title: Tournament selection
concepts.description: Candidates are returned before the next tournament in the described scheme, so the same individual may win repeatedly.

concepts.title: What elitism preserves
concepts.description: Elitism protects the best-so-far value under these assumptions, not a monotonic population average or global optimality.

concepts.title: Pair-level crossover probability
concepts.description: The source applies crossover probability to parent pairs, not independently to every bit.

concepts.title: Single-point crossover trace
concepts.description: Write 10|0101 and 11|1010, then swap the four-bit suffixes.

concepts.title: Remaining source crossover pairs
concepts.description: The cuts are pair-specific: 011|010 with 101|100, and 11|1010 with 10|1100.

concepts.title: Two-point crossover
concepts.description: Two cuts delimit the exchanged segment; the outer segments stay with their original parent.

concepts.title: Alternating multi-point crossover
concepts.description: Multi-point crossover alternates the selected parental segments at the declared cut sites.

concepts.title: Uniform crossover mask
concepts.description: Uniform crossover can choose ownership separately at each position rather than exchanging one contiguous tail.

concepts.title: Per-bit mutation decisions
concepts.description: The mutation probability is tested separately for each bit, with the supplied comparison convention.

concepts.title: Mutation-rate scale
concepts.description: The interval is a lecture guideline, not a proof that every problem’s optimal mutation rate lies within it.

concepts.title: Worked-example settings
concepts.description: Separate the encoded integer range 0…63 from the physical design-variable interval 1…16.

concepts.title: Decode and evaluate the source individual
concepts.description: Decode the genotype into D, map to x, and then evaluate the objective.

concepts.title: Conflicting source normalization
concepts.description: The specified rounded entries sum to 17.57. The earlier 17.51 denominator is inconsistent with them; neither sum should be silently mixed with a different precision convention.

concepts.title: Initial population statistics
concepts.description: Compute population summaries from a consistent set of rounded entries.

concepts.title: Observed versus forced mating pool
concepts.description: The sample favors fitter individuals, but omission in one draw sequence is not the same as zero selection probability.

concepts.title: Expected versus realized mutations
concepts.description: The slide’s arithmetic gives an expected count, not an exact count or a high-certainty one-flip event.

concepts.title: Probability of exactly one mutation
concepts.description: Exactly-one, at-least-one, zero-event probability and expected count are distinct quantities.

concepts.title: Specified fourth-child mutation
concepts.description: Numbering direction must be stated explicitly when applying a bit mutation.

concepts.title: New-generation statistics and rounding
concepts.description: Summing the shown rounded entries gives 20.86; summing exact decoded fitnesses first gives approximately 20.85053. Both yield a mean rounded to 3.48, but their totals are not interchangeable.

concepts.title: Improved population versus exact optimum
concepts.description: The example shows one-generation progress, not completion of the optimization.

concepts.title: Exploration and exploitation
concepts.description: The two extremes have different risks: overexploitation can cause premature convergence and loss of diversity, while excessive exploration can cause stagnation or slow convergence. These are tendencies, not guarantees for every run.

concepts.title: Real coding and numerical precision
concepts.description: Real coding can avoid an explicit bit-grid resolution choice, but ordinary floating-point computation remains finite-precision.

concepts.title: Linear crossover and fitness choice
concepts.description: Generate the prescribed candidates first, then use the declared objective to choose the best two; “best” is not determined by numerical size alone.

concepts.title: Linear crossover and feasibility
concepts.description: The source formulas do not contain bound repair. A declared rejection, repair or other constraint-handling policy is needed.

concepts.title: BLX shift omitted in the printed formula
concepts.description: The printed equation omits −α. Its literal output must remain distinct from the symmetric BLX implementation; the correction is explicit rather than silently substituted.
concepts.subtopic: BLX shift omitted in the printed formula

concepts.title: Symmetric BLX sampling interval
concepts.description: The symmetric interval is [min (P1, P2)−αd, max (P1, P2)+αd], with d=|P2−P1|. This uses the explicitly corrected symmetric convention, not the unshifted printed γ.

concepts.title: SBX spread factor
concepts.description: The spread factor compares child separation with parent separation, not their absolute coordinate values.

concepts.title: SBX density normalization
concepts.description: The two valid-support integrals each equal 0.5, giving unit total probability. Integrating the expanding branch from 0 is not valid.

concepts.title: Inverse-CDF SBX contraction
concepts.description: For r≤0.5, solving 0.5α^(q+1)=r gives α=(2 r)^(1/(q+1)).

concepts.title: Correct expanding cumulative support
concepts.description: The lower limit must be 1 for this expanding density. The printed 0 is an explicit source defect, not a valid alternative convention.

concepts.title: SBX child separation and midpoint
concepts.description: The midpoint-preserving expression is C_±=(P1+P2±α|P2−P1|)/2. The slide’s visually raised distance after α′ is not used as an exponent; multiplication follows from the declared ratio.

concepts.title: Effect of the SBX index
concepts.description: A larger distribution index concentrates offspring nearer the parent values; it does not necessarily place them at the midpoint.

concepts.title: Equal-parent SBX edge case
concepts.description: The ratio definition assumes distinct parents. A separate equal-parent branch preserves the identical values.

concepts.title: Random real-valued mutation
concepts.description: The formula permits offsets from −Δ/2 to +Δ/2. Calling Δ a maximum range does not make it the maximum absolute displacement.

concepts.title: Two polynomial mutation branches
concepts.description: The two symmetric random draws produce equal-magnitude opposite perturbations.

concepts.title: Perturbation and decision bounds
concepts.description: Distinguish the algebraic proposal from a problem-specific constraint-handling policy.

concepts.title: Specified micro-GA scheme
concepts.description: These are parameters of the presented variant, not universal requirements for every small-population GA.

concepts.title: Diversity without bit mutation
concepts.description: Zero ordinary mutation does not mean the whole algorithm lacks a diversity mechanism; restart supplies one.

concepts.title: Population cost versus convergence guarantee
concepts.description: A small population reduces the stated per-generation evaluation count, not necessarily total runtime or online-control suitability.

concepts.title: Four-stage tuning schedule
concepts.description: The scheme changes one parameter at a time and carries forward previously updated values.

concepts.title: Tuning evaluation count
concepts.description: The source contrasts a linear-in-the-number-of-parameters scan budget with the Cartesian product of all candidate values.

concepts.title: Evaluation slots versus distinct settings
concepts.description: Evaluation slots, distinct parameter tuples, and actual objective calls are different counts. In this declared example there are 37 distinct tuples, 40 uncached calls, and 37 perfectly cached calls.

concepts.title: One-at-a-time tuning limitation
concepts.description: Interactions can defeat a single coordinate-wise pass; the lecture itself disclaims a global-optimum guarantee for its limited scan.

concepts.title: Penalty direction
concepts.description: Choose the sign according to objective direction, not arbitrarily from the printed± symbol.

concepts.title: Squared constraint violations
concepts.description: Violation functions are zero on the satisfied side and positive on the violated side; the source penalty sums their squares.

concepts.title: Static, dynamic and adaptive penalties
concepts.description: A schedule depends on generation count; an adaptive rule uses search feedback.

concepts.title: Representation and feasibility in robot planning
concepts.description: The application requires meaningful representation, objective and feasibility evaluation; genetic operators alone do not certify route safety.
